topics.title: What the professional duty of candour requires
topics.summary: Every healthcare professional must be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong with their care that causes, or could cause, harm or distress. The UK healthcare regulators (including the GOC) set this out together in a joint statement on the professional duty of candour.
keyPoints: Tell the patient (or their carer/advocate) when something has gone wrong.
Apologise.
Offer an appropriate remedy or support to put matters right if possible.
Explain fully the short- and long-term effects of what has happened.
Be open and honest with colleagues, employers and regulators; take part in reviews and investigations.
Report adverse incidents and near misses through the right systems so lessons are learned.
The professional duty applies to individuals; there's also a separate statutory duty of candour for organisations (e.g. Regulation 20 in England, overseen by the CQC).
examTraps: Thinking candour only applies when actual harm occurs — it includes potential harm and distress.
Mixing up the professional (individual) duty with the statutory (organisational) duty.
Believing an apology admits legal liability.

diagram.description: Four steps in a row with arrows: Tell → Apologise → Put right / support → Explain effects. Below: 'Report and learn' feeding back into practice.

goDeeper.heading: Examples in optometry
goDeeper.body: Wrong prescription dispensed; lenses glazed with the wrong axis; a missed or delayed referral; a corneal abrasion from contact tonometry; an allergic reaction to drops; records sent to the wrong patient. Each needs honesty with the patient, an apology, practical steps to put it right and reporting.

goDeeper.heading: As a student
goDeeper.body: If something goes wrong in clinic, tell your supervisor straight away — don't try to hide or fix it alone. The supervisor will help with talking to the patient and recording it. Being candid as a student is part of the GOC Standards for Optical Students.

topics.title: Apologising and explaining when things go wrong
topics.summary: A good apology is prompt, sincere and specific, and comes with a clear explanation and a plan. Saying sorry is not an admission of legal liability. Patients mostly want to know what happened, that someone cares, and that it won't happen again.
keyPoints: Apologise as soon as practical, ideally face to face, in a private space.
Be specific: 'I'm sorry that your glasses were made with the wrong prescription.'
Explain what happened in plain language, without jargon or blame.
Say what you'll do now and what support is available.
Listen and answer questions; give a point of contact.
In England and Wales, an apology doesn't of itself amount to an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006, s.2).
Record the conversation and follow up as promised.
examTraps: A non-apology ('I'm sorry you feel that way').
Blaming colleagues or the lab in front of the patient.

diagram.description: Speech bubble template split into parts: 'I'm sorry that…' (specific) → 'What happened was…' (explanation) → 'What we'll do now is…' (remedy) → 'If you have any questions…' (support and contact).

goDeeper.heading: An example conversation
goDeeper.body: 'Mrs Ahmed, thank you for coming back in. I'm sorry — your new glasses were made with the wrong strength in the right lens, which is why things looked blurry. That was our error. We'll remake them as a priority at no cost, and I'll check them myself before you collect. In the meantime your old glasses are safe to use. Do you have any questions? Here's my direct number if anything else worries you.'

goDeeper.heading: After the conversation
goDeeper.body: Record what happened, what you said and agreed, and report the incident through your practice's system. Reflect on it (what caused it, what will prevent it) — it's also good material for CPD reflection once you're qualified.

flashcards.back: Prompt, sincere, specific, with explanation and a plan.
Record it, report the incident, follow up, reflect.

topics.title: Raising concerns
topics.summary: If you're worried that patients could be put at risk — by a colleague, a system, or a practice — you have a professional duty to raise it. Start with the right person locally, keep records, and know where to go if that doesn't work. Whistleblowers are legally protected.
keyPoints: You must raise concerns about patient safety, even as a student.
Start locally: your supervisor, clinic lead or manager; at university, the clinic or programme lead.
If immediate patient safety is at risk, act straight away.
Write down what you saw, when, and who you told.
If local routes fail or aren't appropriate, escalate (e.g. employer's senior management, NHS Freedom to Speak Up Guardians, the regulator).
The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who raise genuine concerns in the public interest.
Concerns about yourself (health, competence) should also be raised — seeking help is professional.
examTraps: Going straight to social media or the press.
Waiting until you have 'proof' when patients are at risk.
Thinking students don't have this duty.

diagram.description: A ladder of escalation from bottom to top: Supervisor or clinic lead → Practice/clinic manager or programme lead → Organisation's senior management or Freedom to Speak Up Guardian → Regulator (e.g. GOC). Side note: if immediate risk, act now.

goDeeper.heading: A student example
goDeeper.body: You notice a practitioner at a placement repeatedly skipping fundus examination on patients with diabetes. Note what you've seen (dates, no patient-identifiable details outside records). Raise it with your placement supervisor or university placement lead. They're there to help you handle it safely and fairly.

goDeeper.heading: Why speaking up matters
goDeeper.body: Many serious failures in healthcare were noticed by someone who felt unable to speak. A culture where people can raise concerns early — without blame — protects patients and staff. Raising a concern is about safety, not about getting someone into trouble.

topics.title: Equality, diversity and inclusion
topics.summary: Your legal and professional duties not to discriminate, how unconscious bias creeps into care, and the reasonable adjustments that make a practice accessible.
keyPoints: GOC standard 13.2: promote equality, value diversity, be inclusive and don't discriminate on any protected characteristic.
Equality Act 2010, nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.

College of Optometrists guidance: don't discriminate against patients (D9) or colleagues (C165). An employer who fails to protect a colleague from racist comments by staff or patients may breach C165.
NHS contracts carry equality obligations, such as the Workforce Race Equality Standard.
Unconscious bias: understand its impact, use logical checks on yourself, and don't become complacent.
Section 20 reasonable adjustments: step-free access, easy-read letters, priority or longer appointments, a quiet waiting space, hearing loops, communication charts for dementia.
examTraps: Listing 'gender' instead of 'sex' and 'gender reassignment' as the Act's protected characteristics.
Using a family member as interpreter without thinking about whether consent is truly informed.
Treating everyone the same and calling it equality: reasonable adjustments mean treating people differently so they get the same access.

goDeeper.heading: Case: a transgender patient
goDeeper.body: A 20-year-old's record says female; he tells you he is transgender and uses he/him, and the receptionist called out his old name. In the room: apologise, use his name and pronouns, and check how he'd like to be recorded. Longer term: update records and systems, train staff, and challenge inappropriate language when you hear it.

goDeeper.heading: Case: language and cultural beliefs
goDeeper.body: A 65-year-old woman new to the UK speaks little English; her son interprets and she is afraid of drops that will 'harm her vision'. Think about professional interpreters, explaining what drops are for (and that they are optional), checking understanding before consent, and whether the son is filtering what she says or hears.
